abstract.p: Algorithmic bias occurs when predictive model performance varies meaningfully across sociodemographic classes, exacerbating systemic healthcare disparities. NYC Health + Hospitals, an urban safety net system, assessed bias in two binary classification models in our electronic medical record: one predicting acute visits for asthma and one predicting unplanned readmissions. We evaluated differences in subgroup performance across race/ethnicity, sex, language, and insurance using equal opportunity difference (EOD), a metric comparing false negative rates. The most biased classes (race/ethnicity for asthma, insurance for readmission) were targeted for mitigation using threshold adjustment, which adjusts subgroup thresholds to minimize EOD, and reject option classification, which re-classifies scores near the threshold by subgroup. Successful mitigation was defined as 1) absolute subgroup EODs <5 percentage points, 2) accuracy reduction <10%, and 3) alert rate change <20%. Threshold adjustment met these criteria; reject option classification did not. We introduce a Supplementary Playbook outlining our approach for low-resource bias mitigation.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: We are on the precipice of an AI and machine learning revolution in healthcare. Algorithms are increasingly augmenting human judgement in diagnostic tasks like cancer identification and prediction of inpatient sepsis while assuming responsibility for repetitive tasks like allocating appointments, staffing, and hospital beds1–4. If all patients are to reap the benefits of these technologies equally, healthcare systems must safeguard equity during their adoption. The digital divide threatens to reach beyond differential access to health technology (i.e., access to electronic medical records, patient portals, telehealth visits) to differential benefit of health technology for some communities over others5.

One way to address digital disparities is by measuring and mitigating algorithmic bias, which arises when predictive model performance varies meaningfully across sociodemographic classes like race or sex6. Bias has been identified in algorithms predicting or measuring opioid misuse7, healthcare cost and utilization8, hypoxemia9, and skin cancer10, among others11. Biased healthcare predictions can preferentially allocate scarce resources according to class membership rather than clinical need12, exacerbating systemic inequities for historically underserved patients11,13–16.

Across the field of machine learning, bias mitigation methods are emerging to meet this challenge. These methods focus on improving fairness within the data on which algorithms are trained (pre-processing); adjusting algorithmic training to prioritize fairness (in-processing); and improving the fairness of algorithmic predictions after deployment (post-processing)4. A growing body of healthcare literature reports pre-processing strategies like reweighting, resampling, label adjustment, and use of synthetic or cross-institutional data; and in-processing methods such as regularization, fairness constraints, and adversarial debiasing10. Fewer studies, however, have examined real-world efficacy of established post-processing approaches like reject option classification (ROC), threshold adjustment, and calibration in healthcare applications. While less widespread, post-processing mitigation methods may be more scalable and less resource-intensive than in- or pre-processing methods as they do not require access to training data or highly skilled developers to deploy16–19.

Methods and standards for bias identification and mitigation are often written for model developers. Healthcare systems, however, are increasingly consumers of predictive models as they are incorporated into electronic medical records (EMRs), personal health devices, and third-party clinical decision support tools. Healthcare systems may see biased local performance even if overall performance is unbiased. An algorithm which performs well on a nationally representative sample may offer biased predictions when run locally on patient populations with different demographic, clinical, and social characteristics. Many healthcare systems lack the expertise and resources to evaluate and adjust these algorithms for bias at the health system level. Within the United States, these technological and staffing barriers are highest at the safety net healthcare systems that predominantly serve historically marginalized communities that are often under-represented in commercial model development and training. Safety net systems have less funding and resources than high-income systems20. Without concrete, easy to implement pathways to identify and mitigate bias, safety net patients will continue to fall behind the innovation curve5,21.

As the largest municipal safety net system in the U.S., New York City Health + Hospitals (H + H) provides an ideal laboratory to test scalable, low-resource approaches to bias identification and mitigation. H + H serves more than 1 million New Yorkers, 90% of whom are patients of color and 70% of whom are covered by Medicaid or lack insurance. Because we serve historically marginalized communities, we are particularly vulnerable to algorithmic bias. In this study, we partnered with local experts to test scalable post-processing approaches to algorithmic bias mitigation that can be implemented across safety nets and other low-resource systems. Specifically, we aimed to 1) identify bias across live clinical algorithms in the H + H electronic medical record; 2) test threshold adjustment and reject option classification, two post-processing mitigation approaches, using open-source tools and custom code made publicly available; and 3) synthesize the most successful, resource-efficient methods and tools into a Supplementary Playbook for other systems to understand and use. While not a panacea for all strains of bias across all algorithms and systems, we offer one strategy as a starting point to fill the accessible mitigation gap in the market. We hope that this evaluation will make practical bias mitigation more achievable for any healthcare system looking to improve digital health equity.

sec.p:

Most asthma model patients identified as Hispanic/Latinx (43.3%) or Black or African American (37.3%). The outcome predicted by the asthma model was 1+ asthma ED or inpatient visits in the year following prediction. In our study, 6.5% of the asthma sample had this outcome (n = 3,476 “cases”). Case population distribution differed significantly from the general model population across race/ethnicity, sex, age, language, and insurance. Asthma prevalence was highest among Black or African American (8.2%) and Hispanic/Latinx patients (6.3%), male patients (7.0%), English speaking patients (6.8%), and patients with Medicaid (7.2%) or Self-Pay (6.4%). On average, cases had significantly more comorbidities ( + 0.3) and ED visits (+ 2.1). Primary and specialty care utilization differences were minimal.

sec.title: Asthma model baseline performance
sec.p:
We measured baseline model performance using AUROC, accuracy, false negative rate (FNR), and alert rate. Full definitions of these terms are provided in Methods, but in brief they measure model discrimination, percent of all predictions that were correct, percent of true positives that were not predicted correctly, and percent predicted positive. Our primary fairness metric was Equal Opportunity Difference (EOD, measuring FNR difference between subgroups and the class referent). An absolute EOD > 5 percentage points (pp) was flagged as biased. At baseline, the asthma model had an AUROC of 0.756, suggesting fair global performance (Table 2). At the 0.15 high risk threshold, asthma had 0.867 accuracy, 0.124 alert rate, and 0.567 FNR. For the baseline asthma model, bias was observed in at least one subgroup of every class except sex (Table 3). Race/ethnicity had the highest within-class burden of bias. At the 0.15 risk threshold, FNR within race/ethnicity ranged from 0.51 (Black or African American) to 0.828 (White). All race/ethnicity subgroups surpassed the absolute EOD >5pp bias threshold. As compared to other classes, race/ethnicity had the worst absolute maximum EOD, crude average EOD, and weighted average EOD. As shown in Table 4, AUROC within race/ethnicity ranged from 0.708 (Asian/NHPI/Native American/Alaskan) to 0.788 (Unknown). Race/ethnicity was selected for mitigation.

sec.title: Asthma model mitigation
sec.p: We mitigated bias using three bias mitigation approaches: custom code threshold adjustment (“custom”), Aequitas-based threshold adjustment (“Aequitas”), and ROC. The results of these mitigation strategies are compared to baseline performance and bias in Tables 2–4.

The new asthma high risk thresholds produced by each mitigation approach are presented in Table 4. While selecting thresholds to minimize EOD, both custom and Aequitas thresholding slightly increased the asthma risk threshold for the highest-performing group (Black or African American) while halving the thresholds for low-performing subgroups. Under the constraints outlined in Methods, the optimal ROC classification threshold for asthma was 0.145 with a region width of 0.695. This increased the high risk threshold for high-performing subgroups (Black or African American and Hispanic/Latinx) from 0.15 to 0.22. For all other groups, ROC decreased the high risk threshold to 0.9.

Custom and Aequitas threshold adjustment both decreased asthma model accuracy slightly, from 0.867 to 0.861 and 0.851, respectively (Table 2). ROC increased accuracy to 0.896. Custom and Aequitas threshold adjustment both increased alert rate from 0.124 to 0.128 and 0.142, respectively, after flipping labels for 1909 and 2046 patients. Although ROC flipped more labels (n = 3811), it decreased alert rate to 0.081.

Within race/ethnicity, the target class for the asthma model, custom threshold adjustment brought all absolute subgroup EODs below the bias threshold of 5pp (Table 4). Custom thresholding also minimized absolute values for all equal opportunity difference metrics for race/ethnicity (Table 3). Although Aequitas thresholding produced non-absolute EODs <5pp for all race/ethnicity subgroups (range: -0.016 to -0.086, with negative values indicating better subgroup FNR than referent), absolute EODs for White and Asian/NHPI subgroups surpassed the 5pp bias threshold. Custom and Aequitas thresholding brought crude absolute average EOD from 0.191 to 0.017 and 0.045, respectively. ROC failed to bring all subgroup EODs below the bias threshold of 5pp. EOD was 0.072 for the Unknown race/ethnicity subgroup, and ranged from -0.041 to -0.078 for other subgroups, indicating that all except Unknown had a better FNR than the referent under ROC. ROC brought crude absolute average EOD to 0.066 for race/ethnicity.

All three mitigation approaches moderately worsened bias in one or more non-target classes (Table 3). All three approaches meaningfully improved bias by language, with the largest reductions observed with custom and Aequitas thresholding. Bias reduction was heterogenous for insurance. ROC improved all EOD metrics for insurance. However, both thresholding approaches produced modest insurance increases in crude and weighted absolute average EOD ( < 0.015). Thresholding approaches slightly increased absolute EOD metrics for sex (≤ 0.01), with larger increases seen for ROC (0.035).

sec.title: Asthma model mitigation outcome
sec.p: Within the asthma model, custom and Aequitas thresholding both met accuracy and alert rate change success criteria when mitigating race/ethnicity bias ( < 10% accuracy and <20% alert rate changes relative to baseline). By dropping alert rate from 0.124 to 0.081, ROC failed the alert rate criteria.

Within the asthma model’s target class, race/ethnicity, custom thresholding successfully brought absolute EOD <5pp for all subgroups. ROC failed to meet this criterion. Aequitas thresholding brought non-absolute race/ethnicity EODs <5pp but did not bring absolute race/ethnicity EODs <5pp.

Among non-target classes, all three approaches modestly increased bias in some EOD metrics for insurance and sex, although bias improved for language. Using absolute EOD metrics, bias impacts were slightly worse using ROC (but still remained ≤3pp).

In sum, asthma mitigation using custom and Aequitas threshold adjustment was a qualified success, requiring contextual investigation within the rendering healthcare organization. ROC cannot be categorized as a qualified success for this use case.

sec.title: Readmission model population overview
sec.p: Characteristics of patients in the readmission model dataset (n = 139,132) are summarized in Table 1. Most readmission model patients identified as Hispanic/Latinx (38.1%) or Black or African American (35.0%). Most patients were older (57.8% >45 years) and preferred English (68.6%) or Spanish (22.7%) as a primary language. Sex was broadly even (52.2% female). Most patients were insured by Medicaid (55.5%) or Medicare (28.5%). Patients had an average of 4.2 chronic diseases documented. At H + H, patients had 1.4 ED visits, 0.8 inpatient visits, 0.7 primary care visits, and 3.7 specialty visits on average in the measurement year.

For readmission, 11.0% of the sample had the outcome of a readmission at H + H within 30 days of discharge (n = 15,342 “cases”). Case population distribution differed significantly from the general model population across race/ethnicity, sex, age, language, and insurance. Readmission prevalence was highest among Black or African American (12.6%) and White patients (11.9%), patients older than 45 (13.4%), male patients (12.7%), English speaking patients (11.8%), and patients with Medicare (14.0%). On average, cases had significantly more average comorbidities ( + 2.4), ED visits ( + 1.4), inpatient visits ( + 0.9), and specialty visits ( + 0.8). Primary care differences were minimal.

sec.title: Readmission model baseline performance
sec.p: At baseline, the readmission model had an AUROC of 0.719, suggesting fair global performance (Table 2). At the 0.17 high risk threshold, the baseline readmission model had 0.750 accuracy, 0.255 alert rate, and 0.478 FNR. Bias ( > 5pp absolute EOD) was observed in at least one subgroup of every class at baseline (Table 3).

Insurance had the highest within-class burden of bias (Table 3). At the 0.17 risk threshold, FNR within insurance ranged from 0.382 (Medicare) to 0.797 (Self-Pay). All insurance subgroups surpassed the absolute EOD >5pp bias threshold. As compared to other classes, insurance had the worst absolute maximum, crude average, and weighted average equal opportunity differences. AUROC within insurance ranged from 0.664 (Self-Pay) to 0.735 (Medicaid) (Table 4). Insurance was selected for mitigation.

sec.title: Readmission model mitigation
sec.p: The new readmission high risk thresholds produced by each mitigation approach are presented in Table 4. While selecting thresholds to minimize EOD, both custom and Aequitas thresholding slightly increased the readmission risk threshold for the highest-performing group (Medicare) while reducing the thresholds for low-performing subgroups. Under the constraints outlined in Methods, the optimal ROC classification threshold for readmission was 0.167 with a region width of 0.044. This increased the risk threshold for high-performing subgroups (Medicare, Medicaid) from 0.17 to 0.22. For all other groups, ROC decreased the high risk threshold to 0.13.

Aequitas threshold adjustment decreased readmission model accuracy slightly, from 0.750 to 0.746 (Table 2). Custom threshold adjustment and ROC both increased accuracy, to 0.754 and 0.803, respectively. Aequitas threshold adjustment increased alert rate from 0.255 to 0.258, after flipping labels for 7229 patients. Custom threshold adjustment decreased alert rate to 0.247, flipping 8,485 labels. ROC decreased alert rate to 0.174, flipping 16,042 labels.

Within insurance, the target class for the readmission model, custom threshold adjustment brought all absolute subgroup EODs below the 5pp bias threshold (Table 4). Using absolute EOD, Aequitas and ROC both surpassed the 5pp bias threshold in at least one insurance subgroup. Using non-absolute values, all three approaches produced some negative subgroup EODs for insurance – Aequitas and ROC more than custom – indicating better FNRs in a given subgroup than the referent (Table 4). All three methods brought crude absolute average EOD for insurance below 5pp, ranging from 0.017 (custom) to 0.048 (ROC, Table 3). Weighted absolute average EODs for insurance were <5pp for crude and Aequitas adjustment but 0.061 for ROC.

All three mitigation approaches moderately worsened bias in one or more non-target classes (Table 3). All three approaches worsened bias by sex and meaningfully improved bias by race, with the largest reductions observed in thresholding methods. Bias reduction was heterogenous for language. All three methods improved biggest absolute EOD and crude absolute average EOD for language. Both thresholding methods worsened weighted average EOD for language (0.70 to 0.72) while ROC did not change it.

sec.title: Readmission Model Mitigation Outcome
sec.p: Custom and Aequitas thresholding both met accuracy and alert rate change success criteria for readmission ( < 10% accuracy and <20% alert rate changes relative to baseline). By changing alert rate from 0.255 to 0.174, ROC failed the alert rate criteria.

Within the readmission model’s target class, insurance, custom thresholding brought absolute EOD to <5pp for all subgroups. Aequitas and ROC brought non-absolute EOD to <5pp but failed to bring absolute EOD to <5pp for all insurance subgroups.

Among non-target classes, all three approaches improved bias for race and language by most metrics. Both thresholding methods modestly increased weighted absolute average EOD for language ( < 2pp). All three approaches slightly increased bias for sex ( < 2pp).

In sum, for the readmission model, custom and Aequitas threshold adjustment were qualified successes, requiring contextual investigation within the rendering healthcare organization. Custom thresholding minimized EOD metrics more than Aequitas thresholding. ROC cannot be categorized as a qualified success, due to its changes to alert rate.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In a real-world trial of post-processing bias mitigation, threshold adjustment emerged as the simplest and strongest method to address equal opportunity difference within two clinical classification algorithms in the NYC Health + Hospitals electronic medical record. Both threshold adjustment approaches reduced non-absolute EOD for the target class to <5pp for asthma (race/ethnicity) and readmission (insurance) while yielding minimal changes in accuracy or alert rate. Custom threshold adjustment is the only approach that reduced every target class subgroup’s absolute EOD to <5pp, indicating all subgroup FNRs fall within 5pp of the reference group. For asthma and readmission, custom thresholding showed greater target class reductions across the single biggest EOD, crude average EOD, and weighted average EOD. For non-target classes, thresholding approaches either improved or slightly worsened EOD ( < 1.5pp), yielding a qualified success. ROC failed to bring all target class subgroups for asthma below the bias threshold of 5pp and decreased alert rate by >30% for both models, failing to meet success criteria. For both its accessibility and superior impact on bias reduction, custom-coded threshold adjustment emerged as the best algorithmic bias mitigation method for these clinical classification algorithm use cases.

Our results support emerging findings in the nascent literature on post-processing bias mitigation in healthcare. Across a family of threshold adjustment approaches, similar reductions in bias with low to no accuracy loss (where reported) were seen across studies by Gianattasio (2020), Hardt (2016), Jang (2022), Mishler (2021), Rodolfa (2021), Small (2023), Tahir (2023), and Thompson (2021) et al., although Lohia et al. (2019) found no bias reduction7,22–29. For ROC approaches, reductions in bias with low to no accuracy loss (where reported) were observed across studies by Briggs (2020), Kamiran (2012), Lohia (2019), Tahir (2023), and Tubella (2022) et al., while Nguyen et al. (2021) found mixed to no bias reduction using ROC methods17,25,29–32. Our study was one of few we identified25,29 to compare the performance of these methods head-to-head, and the only one to do so using safety net data. Health informatics research is largely conducted at well-resourced academic medical centers33. Studies using safety net data contribute learnings on advancing digital health equity in patient pools where historically underserved populations become the “average” patient.

Of the 16 bias mitigation software libraries we identified in our literature review, we tested functionality in Aequitas (threshold adjustment) and AIF360 (ROC)34,35. We chose these libraries because they offered post-processing bias mitigation functionality and were at least theoretically accessible using R, a coding language commonly used in healthcare. An additional advantage of both toolkits is that they only required prediction, outcome, and class variable data for post-processing mitigation, lowering the barrier to entry. Despite their pre-existing, open-source appeal, however, we found Aequitas and AIF360 lacked documentation and adaptability. Navigating dense, outdated open-source libraries was arduous for our team of R and Python analysts, despite our access to machine learning expertise from our collaborators at NYU. We found documentation was often outdated and opaque or written for a level of expertise beyond that of an average analyst. We have provided lessons learned for Aequitas in our study code repository for system analysts with Python skills. Ultimately, we found our own in-house R code to be more efficient to use, providing better transparency than Aequitas and AIF360 while yielding comparable or superior fairness gains.

Algorithmic bias mitigation is one important piece of a holistic health equity strategy which transparently addresses health system challenges and incorporates patients as decision-makers. Trust in health systems is at an all-time low post-pandemic, with 64% of Black or African American patients citing bias as a major problem in modern healthcare36,37. Patients are concerned about whether algorithms and AI are being deployed fairly and accurately. In a nationally representative survey issued in 2019, nearly 96% of patients wanted to be informed about the use of algorithms in their medical care, and 92% of patients were concerned about receiving a misdiagnosis from a decision-support tool38. In a 2023 Pew survey, 60% of Americans reported feeling uncomfortable about the idea of AI influencing diagnostic decisions37. As predictive models are integrated across clinical applications, transparently minimizing algorithmic bias in every healthcare system is essential for strengthening trust in medicine. Post-processing methods like threshold adjustment may make this goal more achievable.

A primary aim of this project was to disseminate our findings in a way that would be scalable for other low-resource health systems, lowering the barrier to entry for practical mitigation of algorithmic bias. Our comparative analysis of three post-processing approaches found custom threshold adjustment to be effective and relatively easy to implement. We have written a Supplementary Playbook on how to implement threshold adjustment in practice, providing step-by-step instructions using real-world examples (Supplementary Playbook 1). The Supplementary Playbook is accompanied by a public, open-source R code repository which can be modified and deployed across other systems.

We are not the first health system to develop algorithmic bias mitigation guidelines, but to our knowledge, we are among the first to publish them. Many authors call for the need for standards4,16,39–43. When developing our Supplementary Playbook, however, we found a paucity of publicly available guidelines to flag unacceptable levels of bias or identify which sensitive class should be mitigated for bias. In our Supplementary Playbook, we provide a starter set of standards which systems can tailor locally to fit their own equity goals and challenges. We pair these standards with realistic implementation pathways to adjust thresholds within the electronic medical record. It is our hope that the Supplementary Playbook offers one achievable path which health systems can follow, regardless of resources, to limit algorithmic bias and improve equity (Supplementary Playbook 1).

Our Supplementary Playbook is not a panacea for addressing all forms of bias in healthcare technology. Bias is multifactorial and can be introduced at any stage of the algorithmic lifecycle16,40,43. For example, data are often systematically missing or mislabeled in the EMR for some subgroups6. The Elixhauser comorbidity index imbedded within this study’s readmission model is likely more complete for insured patients than uninsured patients, because uninsured patients may under-utilize care, particularly preventive care, thereby missing opportunities to diagnose and document chronic conditions44. Poor selection of training samples, feature selection bias, and label bias can be resistant to post-processing mitigation methods and may require model redevelopment16,40. As outlined in Obermeyer et al.’s foundational 2021 bias playbook, a robust approach to algorithmic fairness requires identifying the true outcome of interest, looking at patterns of missing data and investigating sources of bias at the development, deployment and monitoring phases, while prioritizing transparency and the inclusion of patient voices. This study did not impute missing data, which is a limitation that should be addressed in future research. Our Supplementary Playbook outlines one tool among many which systems can deploy within a holistic approach to digital equity (Supplementary Playbook 1).

Our study may also have more limited generalizability outside of safety net systems and the EMR-based algorithms studied. The catchment area of H + H is unique, and findings are particularly relevant to low-income, safety net patient populations. Although we began our study with a range of algorithms covering inpatient, ED, and outpatient settings, we ultimately retained only asthma and readmission models. Threshold adjustment and ROC mitigation may perform differently across algorithms with frequent, real-time predictions such as sepsis prediction models. There is no optimal fairness metric for all use cases identified in the literature10. We optimized for equal opportunity difference, but findings would likely change if we were to select another metric. The thresholding approach we selected for our Supplementary Playbook is relatively straightforward to deploy and evaluate (Supplementary Playbook 1). However, using threshold adjustment to address intersectional bias may produce exponentially increasing thresholds based on number of crossed subgroups which may prove difficult to implement within routine clinical practice. Future research should invest in identifying post-processing methods with capacity to address intersectional biases, adjusting for multiple sensitive classes beyond a single-axis45. Finally, this study outlined a pathway to successfully mitigate algorithmic bias in two clinical classification algorithms within the EMR, but the most important test of these methods will be their ability to impact the allocation of interventions and associated outcome improvements in practice. Implementation research is needed to grow the evidence base for the real-world impact of thresholding and similar post-processing methods on health equity.

sec.title: Models
sec.p:
We sought to test threshold adjustment and ROC bias mitigation approaches using commercially available models within our safety net. Figure 1 outlines our model selection process. Five cognitive computing models met the inclusion criterion of ≥1 year of prediction and associated outcome data within in the NYC Health + Hospitals EMR system. These included Risk of Emergency Department Visit or Hospitalization (“acute utilization”) for Asthma (“asthma”), Risk of Unplanned Readmission (“readmit,” version 1), Risk of Patient No-Show (“no-show,” version 1), Inpatient Risk of Falls (“falls”), and Deterioration Index (“DI”)44. Model-level global performance exclusion criteria included poor performance, defined as area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) < 70% and area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC) < 10%46. DI and no-show models were excluded with AUROC 64.11% and 67.86%, respectively. Falls was excluded with PR-AUC 0.78%, indicating trivial predictive value. Asthma and readmit were retained for bias identification and mitigation analysis (AUROC 75.56%, PR-AUC 26.73% asthma; AUROC 71.85%, PR-AUC 24.93% readmit). Both retained algorithms were logistic regression models used for clinical classification tasks. Our system’s primary use case for both retained models was automated outreach to high-risk patients through the patient portal to prompt outpatient appointment scheduling and follow-up. If biased, prompts from these algorithms could lead to differential outpatient visit access by sociodemographic group within a resource-limited safety net system.Fig. 1Algorithmic Bias Identification and Mitigation Process.
Figure 1 illustrates the workflow for our algorithmic bias identification and mitigation process. Step 1: We began by identifying a list of the classification models generating risk predictions within our electronic medical record system to consider for bias identification and mitigation (eight models). All models with at least one year’s worth of prediction and outcome data were considered eligible for performance evaluation (five models). Step 2: Models with AUROC > 70% and PR-AUC > 10% were considered eligible for bias assessment (two models). Step 3: Bias was assessed within and across sociodemographic classes of interest. Models with equal opportunity difference (EOD) > 5 percentage points within one or more classes were considered biased (two models). Across classes, the class with the highest burden of bias as measured by EOD metrics was targeted for mitigation for each model. Step 4: Three methods of mitigation were tested on each model: threshold adjustment using custom code, threshold adjustment using the Aequitas library, and reject option classification. Step 5: After each mitigation technique was applied to each model, model performance and bias assessment (Steps 2 and 3) were repeated to assess changes to model performance and reductions in bias.

sec.title: Eligible patients
sec.p: Predictions, outcomes, and patient characteristics were extracted from the H + H Epic EMR Clarity database from July 2024 to November 2024. The reporting year was defined as the most recent year of outcome data with associated available prediction data: July 29, 2023 to July 28, 2024 for asthma; August 10, 2022 to August 9, 2023 for readmit. Patients with documented race/ethnicity, sex, language, and insurance status were eligible for inclusion. Patients included in the asthma cohort were aged 18+ years with a primary diagnosis of asthma; no recorded COPD, emphysema, or chronic bronchitis; and a qualifying in-person ambulatory encounter during the reporting period plus an additional ambulatory, ED, or inpatient visit in the two years preceding the reporting period (n = 53,099 patients). Patients included in the readmit cohort were aged >12 months with an inpatient visit during the reporting period with any discharge status except hospice or deceased (n = 139,132 patients).

sec.title: Predictions
sec.p: Asthma predictions are stored in the Epic EMR as a continuous risk score (0 to 1) at the patient level. Our system retains only the current risk score for each patient, so this study retroactively calculated the historical, point-in-time risk scores eligible patients would have received on the first date of the reporting period (July 29th 2023). We used Epic’s recommended risk threshold of 0.15 to flag “high risk” patients, capturing 12.4% of the asthma cohort44.

Readmit predictions are stored in the Epic EMR as continuous risk scores (0 to 1) at the encounter level. All patients included in the readmit dataset were matched to the last risk score generated prior to discharge for that patient’s final encounter during the reporting period. We used Epic’s recommended risk threshold of 0.17 to flag “high risk” patients, capturing 25.5% of the readmit cohort44.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: For asthma, the outcome of interest was 1+ acute visits in the year following the point-in-time risk score (July 29, 2023). This captured 3,476 patients (“cases”). For readmit, the outcome of interest was 1+ inpatient admissions to any of the 11 H + H hospitals within 30 days of discharge from the final inpatient visit of the reporting period. This captured 15,342 patients (“cases”).

sec.title: Sensitive classes
sec.p: System context, key informant interviews, and a review of the literature informed our selection of sociodemographic classes18, yielding race/ethnicity, sex, preferred language, and insurance status. Age was determined to be a significant outcome mediator with clinical implications for disease trajectory for both readmit and asthma, and was not retained for bias analysis. Sexual orientation and gender identity were unreliably collected in our study data and were not included in the analysis. To ensure adequate subgroup sample size, we collapsed and removed some subgroups within classes. Subgroups comprising less than 1% of their respective class were combined with similar subgroups within that class or dropped if no logical combinations existed. Refer to Table 1 for the full enumeration of final subgroups across race/ethnicity, sex, language, and insurance classes. The largest subgroup served as the referent for each class, including Hispanic/Latinx (race/ethnicity), female (sex), Medicaid (insurance), and English (language).

sec.title: Analysis
sec.p: Data were pulled using SQL Management Studio (version 19) and analyzed using RStudio (R 4.2.3) and Jupyter Notebooks (Python 3.9.14). Table 1 compares asthma and readmit cohorts by case status across sociodemographics (race/ethnicity, sex, age, preferred language, insurance status); comorbidity (average Elixhauser score), and utilization (average visits to primary care, specialty care, ED, and inpatient visits from the relevant year of patient-level data). Significance was assessed with t-tests (averages) and chi squared tests (distributions) at p < 0.05.

Fairness metrics were used to identify bias at baseline within and across sensitive classes for each algorithm. Using Paulus and Kent’s decision logic and Aequitas’ fairness guidance, we selected equal opportunity as the primary fairness metric for our use case of automated messaging to high-risk patients34,40. Equal opportunity difference was calculated as subgroup false negative rate (FNR) minus referent group FNR. Fairness metrics must be matched appropriately to use case needs. If the model use case is punitive (harms false positives) or resource intensive (costly to the system), equal opportunity may not be optimal. For example, an H + H acute utilization algorithm which connects patients to enhanced care management would be better assessed using predictive parity to ensure that limited safety net resources are not directed to patients who are less likely to benefit from them47. Equal opportunity was the best fit for our use case because automated messaging is assistive in nature (no harm in reaching out to a false positive patient) and not resource intensive (does not cost the system much). Predictive parity difference (PPV subgroup minus PPV referent) was calculated as a secondary fairness metric.

To assess within-class bias at baseline and after each mitigation approach, we calculated FNR, EOD, and PPV for all subgroups within each class. In Table 2, we report EOD, FNR, and PPV for the target class at baseline and after mitigation. We also report accuracy (percent of correct predictions over total predictions), alert rate (percent predicted high risk), and label flips (number of classification changes produced during mitigation). Subgroup AUROC is presented as a threshold-agnostic measure of performance. We calculated but declined to report bootstrapped 95% Agresti-Coull confidence intervals7,22 for FNR and PPV. These confidence intervals were highly impacted by subgroup sample size, flagging comparable levels of bias as both significant and not significant based on demographic dominance of a given subgroup. We felt this approach would disadvantage small minority groups in this evaluation.

Looking at bias across classes to identify the target class for mitigation, we sought to balance magnitude of disparity in each subgroup with level of disparity across subgroups. Table 3 reports EOD measures by class, including (1) the biggest absolute EOD observed within the class; (2) the crude average of absolute EOD across subgroups; (3) the average of absolute EOD weighted by subgroup size; and (4) percent of subgroups with absolute EOD >5pp, derived from Gianatassio et al. 22. The class with the largest absolute EOD across a plurality of these measures was targeted for mitigation (“target class”).

An extended umbrella review identified threshold adjustment and reject option classification as computationally efficient and accuracy-preserving methods to mitigate bias within off-the-shelf clinical classification models4. This review also surfaced AIF360 and Aequitas as the most popular open-source libraries with post-processing methods applicable to binary predictive models34,35. We set out to test these two bias mitigation approaches, using novel custom and existing library code.

We used the Aequitas Python library to perform ‘balanced’ group threshold adjustment. Within a sociodemographic class, threshold adjustment selects subgroup-specific thresholds to minimize a chosen fairness metric, in this case equal opportunity difference. To identify operational or computational advantages of using the Aequitas toolkit, we also tested threshold adjustment using custom R code written in-house. The two methods are comparable, but our custom code allowed subgroup fairness metrics to fall above or below the referent, while Aequitas forces all subgroup metrics above the referent.

We tested ROC using AIF360, augmented with the Sony nnbala Python library35,48. Due to the complexity of ROC implementation, we did not develop custom code for this approach. ROC requires subgroups to be collapsed into binary high-performing (“privileged”) and low-performing (“unprivileged”) groups. ROC identifies a classification threshold that optimizes accuracy and minimizes chosen fairness metric difference between privileged and unprivileged groups30. It then calculates a symmetrical “ROC region” around the classification threshold within which predictions are assumed to have greatest likelihood of misclassification. ROC reclassifies the predictions for privileged and unprivileged patients who fall within the ROC region. This is called label flipping (i.e., ROC flips “low risk” unprivileged patient to “high risk” and “high risk” privileged patient to “low risk”).

In our study, all subgroups with an FNR equal to or better than the referent were combined with the referent into the “privileged” group. For asthma, privileged groups were Black or African American and Hispanic/Latinx; for readmit, privileged groups were Medicare and Medicaid. All other subgroups were combined into “unprivileged” groups. We constrained our classification thresholds to the initial thresholds (0.15 asthma, 0.17 readmit) to ensure the affected individuals were localized to a region that would provide clinical utility and comparable alert rates.

Mitigation methods passing Criteria 1 and 2 were graded on Criteria 3 as a success, no success, or a qualified success. Success was defined as improvement or no change in EOD metrics across all non-targeted classes. No success was defined as substantive increases in EOD ( ≥ 2pp) across metrics in one or more non-target classes. Qualified success was defined as moderate increases in EOD (< 2pp) in some metrics in one or more non-target classes.

sec.title: Inclusion and ethics
sec.p: This study was classified as exempt by the BRANY Institutional Review Board in accordance with 45 CFR 46.104(d), which deemed it secondary research. The data included in this research was highly specific to the local context, as were the staff and collaborators, all New York City Health + Hospitals, New York University, and NYU Grossman School of Medicine researchers. New York City Health + Hospitals Equity & Access Council and Predictive Analytics Governance Council were included in key decision-making for this project, including selection of protected classes, sensitive variables, and model use cases determining contextually specific metrics for measuring fairness. Patient councils will be involved in the implementation phase of this project.
